deter

/dih-TUR/ - rhymes with occur · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Deter means to put someone off an action by making its consequences seem too risky.

Two llamas graze with the flock because their size and temper deter the coyotes that ignore every fence.

Example

Midway through the season the league doubled the suspension for a head-high tackle and began printing every ban in the match program. Tackles of that kind fell by half before a single new suspension was served. The commissioners had not caught more offenders; the new price had deterred them, changing the arithmetic in each player's head at the moment of the lunge.

Deter is the exact word for what the new rule did, because to deter is to put someone off an action by making its consequences seem too risky — the decision dies before the act. Discourage, this unit's gentler cousin, merely damps enthusiasm; deter posts a price. Nobody was talked out of tackling. They read the bill for it and declined.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

dissuade: Dissuade means to talk someone out of an action — the tool is argument, and it works face to face. Deter needs no conversation at all: it posts a price, a fine or a camera or a llama, and lets fear of the consequences do the persuading from a distance.

scare off: To scare off is the blunt everyday cousin of deter: the fear works out in the open, and the scared party usually bolts on the spot. Deter is cooler and earlier — the consequences are weighed in advance, and the act quietly never gets chosen.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

embolden: shrinks the risk in someone's eyes until the act looks safe

invite: makes the act look welcome, or at least unwatched

Where it sits · how completely the act gets blocked

discourage → deter → prevent

discourage vs. deter: Discourage is the soft pedal, well short of deter — a sigh, a long form, a raised eyebrow; the act stays open, it just loses its shine, and no price is ever posted.

prevent vs. deter: Prevent goes further than deter — a deterred trespasser decides not to climb; a prevented one climbs and meets a wall he cannot top.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-: away from

Root — ter: to frighten (Latin terrere)

Put it together: De- (away from) + ter (to frighten) = to frighten away from. Latin deterrere was exactly that: scaring someone back from a course. English trimmed the root to a single syllable, but the fright is still doing the work — what deters you is the flash of what could go wrong.

Use the root in a new word: terrify: One low growl from beyond the firelight was enough to terrify the whole camping party into a single tent.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / practical

Deter is for consequences that do the persuading: fines, cameras, llamas. Its noun is this unit's deterrence, the standing policy of it. Discourage — met again in this unit's reference list — is milder, damping the wish without naming a price, and prevent belongs to walls and locks, which stop the act instead of the appetite. And keep deter clear of defer, its sound-alike: deferring only moves an appointment.
